III. The Zoroastrian Light of Glory (Xvarnah) and Angelology
passage-en-00558

But how is all this to become an event for him, his own event? This is what Suhrawardi will describe in symbolic stories that unfold the great themes of the mystical epic. Their settings and their dramatis personae, the characters who take part, presuppose that he has introduced his disciple to the hierarchy of being and, with it, to the hierarchies of beings of light.
III. The Zoroastrian Light of Glory (Xvarnah) and Angelology
passage-en-00559

Of these, the one nearest the disciple will become his guide, if he proves worthy, for that being too has its origin in the Orient of the Lights (origo-oriens), at the sources of the Light of Glory and of the Sovereignty of Light. In broad outline, then, what is at issue is Suhrawardi’s fundamental angelology: fundamental because it provides the structure through which being is understood and through which being reveals itself to consciousness.
III. The Zoroastrian Light of Glory (Xvarnah) and Angelology
en-book-2-ch-3-s3
3. The Archangelic Lights and the Platonic Ideas
III. The Zoroastrian Light of Glory (Xvarnah) and Angelology
passage-en-00560

Ideally, we would set out the whole of Suhrawardi’s angelology here. We must confine ourselves to its essential features. We need to keep in mind the order in which its figures arise, and remember what Suhrawardi means by the world of Darkness.
III. The Zoroastrian Light of Glory (Xvarnah) and Angelology
passage-en-00561

We must clarify the words he uses for the beings of light that he identifies with the Platonic Ideas. In fact, however, his Ideas are no longer quite the same as Plato’s, because Suhrawardi understands them through an angelology explicitly related to that of Zoroastrianism. The later Neoplatonists, on the other hand—Proclus and Damascius, commentators on the Chaldean Oracles—would have recognised much that was familiar.
III. The Zoroastrian Light of Glory (Xvarnah) and Angelology
passage-en-00562
We must then sketch the structure of the hierarchies of Light that eternally proceed from the Light of Lights.
III. The Zoroastrian Light of Glory (Xvarnah) and Angelology
passage-en-00563
Finally, we must grasp what this angelology means for the spiritual life actually lived by the visionary theosopher, for his sacred way of being—his “hieratic” ethos.
III. The Zoroastrian Light of Glory (Xvarnah) and Angelology
passage-en-00564

As we have already explained, visionary perception identifies the Xvarnah—the Light of Glory, flaming Majesty, the Energy that holds together the being of every creature and surrounds it with its fire beyond the senses, its “personal angel” and its “destiny”—as the source of the Light that is identical with being itself, the Orient of all Light and the Light of every Orient. From this Light of Glory comes the name given to the highest Lights, which proceed immediately from it and mediate its power to the weaker Lights. They are the Anwâr qâhira, the “victorial” Lights.
III. The Zoroastrian Light of Glory (Xvarnah) and Angelology
passage-en-00565

The Arabic qâhira corresponds to the Persian pîrûz; it indicates that their being unites the two qualities called xvarrômand and râyômand in Pahlavi (see above, p. 100), qualities belonging to beings invested with the Light of Glory and the sovereignty of Light. We also often call them “archangelic Lights,” because the dawning Lights—the primordial Ishrâqât—which proceed directly from the Orient of the Lights are literally Archangels (Ru’asâ’ al-Malakût al-Qâhira). In the word archangel, the Greek arkhê evokes both beginning or first principle and command or supremacy.
III. The Zoroastrian Light of Glory (Xvarnah) and Angelology
passage-en-00566

Moreover, the very idea of an archangelic order completes an image that accords with the chivalric ethic developed, on different planes of existence, by Zoroastrian angelology. There is the struggle of the powers of Light supporting Ohrmazd, who is Wisdom-Light. There is also the struggle of the Fravartis (Persian forûhar), heavenly beings who are the archetypes of every creature of light. Their name means, literally, “those who have chosen”: those who chose to descend into the material world to fight the opposing Ahrimanian powers.
III. The Zoroastrian Light of Glory (Xvarnah) and Angelology
passage-en-00567

We find the same indication even in the name Suhrawardi chooses for the Lights that govern bodies. He calls each one a Light (Nûr) Espahbad, using an ancient military title whose very sound recalls the deeds of Iran’s chivalry (see also Chapter V below). Earlier we recalled how the traditional Christian image of the Angel derived, chiefly through Gnostic intermediaries, from the representations of Nike, or “Victories,” in Greek sculpture.
III. The Zoroastrian Light of Glory (Xvarnah) and Angelology
passage-en-00568

Angelus victor, Lux victorialis, invicta: the “archangelic Lights” thus manifest the same quality expressed by the name Mons Victorialis, the mountain rising from Lake Hâmûn in Sistan. For this lake—the Kansaoya Lake of the Avesta—is a receptacle of the Xvarnah, and its image is associated with the Saoshyant to come, the Saviour who will be “victorious.”
III. The Zoroastrian Light of Glory (Xvarnah) and Angelology
passage-en-00569

We also recalled earlier (p. 65 above) how the first illumination and the first reflection of the Light of Lights, or Light of Glory, gave rise to the original relationship of the First Beloved and the First Lover. This twofold relationship is inherent in the eternal phenomenon of Light, in which the revelation of being itself takes place, since being and light are ultimately the same.
III. The Zoroastrian Light of Glory (Xvarnah) and Angelology
passage-en-00570

If being, in its depths, means Light and the Sovereignty of Light, its disclosure and its various forms can occur only through a hierarchy of degrees, a progressive diminishing of Light. It is because Light is not only the source of all sovereignty but is sovereignty itself that some beings have power over others, and the latter are subordinate to the former. Such predominance and subordination express—and are fundamentally determined by—one thing: the relationship between different intensities of Light, stronger in some beings and weaker in others. This relation provides the pattern by which the Many proceed from the One. It is the very pattern of the fundamental angelology of the Ishrâq, of Suhrawardi’s philosophy, replacing the Peripatetic and Avicennian schemes.
III. The Zoroastrian Light of Glory (Xvarnah) and Angelology
passage-en-00571

At every level it is essentially a relationship of love. Each more intense Light has power over a less intense Light—reigning over it like a beloved who commands love, through the attraction it exerts—while the lesser Light longs for it and turns towards it. These are the two “dimensions,” qahr and mahabbat, reflected in Suhrawardi’s rich vocabulary: sovereignty of Light (tasallot nûrî), dominion through manifestation (Qahr zohûrî), divine radiance (bâriq ilâhî), and so on.
III. The Zoroastrian Light of Glory (Xvarnah) and Angelology
passage-en-00572

All these images arise from the concept of the Light of Glory (Xvarnah) revealing itself in the many Ishrâqât, the dawning Lights or illuminations. This is the relationship we find at the eternal dawn of being, between the Light of Lights and the primordial Archangel whom Suhrawardi calls by his Zoroastrian name, Bahman (Avestan Vohu Manah, Good Thought; Greek Eunoia).
III. The Zoroastrian Light of Glory (Xvarnah) and Angelology
passage-en-00573

That is why, as we have already pointed out, when Suhrawardi invokes “the sage Empedocles,” we must be careful not to confuse qahr and mahabbat, as understood by the new Empedocles known to Islamic Gnostics, with “love” and “strife” in the classical Empedocles. For Suhrawardi, qahr is fundamentally the dominion, the hold the beloved has over the lover, so richly explored in the mystical poetry of Persia. Mahabbat is the movement of love that directs the lover towards the beloved and places the lover in dependence upon the beloved, just as an effect is ordered towards and dependent upon its cause. For it is the cause’s illumination, dawning upon the effect, that raises the effect into being.
III. The Zoroastrian Light of Glory (Xvarnah) and Angelology
passage-en-00574

“Know,” writes Suhrawardi, “that every cause whose nature is light feels towards its effect both love (mahabbat) and sovereign superiority (qahr), while the effect feels towards its cause a love inseparable from a sense of dependence (dhill). That is why all being appears arranged in pairs, corresponding to the differing degrees of light and darkening, dominion and love: the superior rank that belongs to the power of dominion over what is lower, and the sense of dependence inherent in love towards what is higher. As God Most High says: ‘Of every being We have made a pair; perhaps you will take heed’ (51:49).”
III. The Zoroastrian Light of Glory (Xvarnah) and Angelology
passage-en-00575

How, then, does the universe appear to the shaykh al-Ishrâq, beginning with the physical world? As an immense succession of dwelling places and steps marking the stages in the diminishing of Light, down to its burial in pure Darkness. Every movement of love, at whatever level and in whatever form, is the longing of a being to rise again out of this fall, calling upon the power of the Light that precedes and rules over it. So, step by step, the redemption of Light takes place through love, which is also the anguish of Light in exile—an anguish that only the “victorial” strength of the higher Light can overcome, calling the exiled Light back to itself.
III. The Zoroastrian Light of Glory (Xvarnah) and Angelology
passage-en-00576

In broad outline, the physics of Eastern Theosophy teaches us the following. Some things are, in their fundamental reality, Light, brightness, and splendour; others are, in their fundamental reality, Darkness, obscurity, and night. Light can be an accidental quality of something other than itself—a thing of which it is, precisely, the light.
III. The Zoroastrian Light of Glory (Xvarnah) and Angelology
passage-en-00577

Or it can be a substance existing in and through itself, as do the archangelic Lights of the different orders and the Souls governing bodies of various kinds. Similarly, Darkness may refer to the degree of darkness present in a thing, or it may mean bodily substance itself, which as such is inert and devoid of light and life. For this Suhrawardi uses the term barzakh, suggesting an in-between space, a screen, or an interval.
III. The Zoroastrian Light of Glory (Xvarnah) and Angelology
passage-en-00578

For the Ishrâqîyûn, a body is neither an assembly of atoms nor a compound of matter and form, as it is for the Peripatetic philosophers who follow Aristotle’s matter-and-form theory. Broadly speaking, a body is anything that forms a screen, anything that obstructs the Light and can, by that very fact, receive it and become a place where it appears (mazhar). A “body,” then, is whatever remains as pure, inert, undifferentiated Darkness once the Light has withdrawn from it.
III. The Zoroastrian Light of Glory (Xvarnah) and Angelology
passage-en-00579

We should note that for Suhrawardi there is no “neutral state,” no condition that is neither Light nor Darkness. Here his physics differs from that of the Peripatetics. For the latter, the withdrawal or absence of Light is not enough to make a thing dark. The thing must also possess the potential to receive Light. Air, for example—meaning cosmic space—cannot be called dark. It is transparent: it lets light pass through without stopping or reflecting it, as a barzakh does. Light simply cannot belong to it as a quality.
III. The Zoroastrian Light of Glory (Xvarnah) and Angelology
passage-en-00580

The Ishrâqîyûn, on the other hand, extend the meaning of Darkness beyond even the concept of barzakh, insisting, on the authority of the ancient sages, that Air or cosmic space must be called dark. For anything that is neither Light in itself nor a receptacle of Light is Darkness. This includes a barzakh once the Light has left it, and Air, which cannot even receive Light in the relevant sense.
III. The Zoroastrian Light of Glory (Xvarnah) and Angelology
passage-en-00581

We can only say that there are some barzakhs from which Light never withdraws—the sun and stars—and others from which it withdraws, temporarily or for good. It follows that barzakhs can never, of themselves, be the cause of anything. They differ from one another only through the Light that comes to them like a stranger living in exile. That Light owes none of its existence to their dark substance, since nothing can bring into being something higher than itself.
III. The Zoroastrian Light of Glory (Xvarnah) and Angelology
passage-en-00582

However closely we examine things, we find nothing other than Light as either their remote or their immediate cause. Motion and heat, for example, are two ways in which Light manifests itself (mazhar). Light causes them, not the other way around. Motion and heat “prepare” a receptacle for Light to become actual within it. That Light, flowing from the “victorial Light” (Nûr qâhir), will correspond to the capacity that has developed in the receptacle—a capacity whose original cause is, again, none other than Light. For Light brings heat and motion into existence. By its very essence it is active and pours itself forth (fa’âl, fayyâz). Light needs only to exist in order to illuminate; no new agent has to intervene.
III. The Zoroastrian Light of Glory (Xvarnah) and Angelology
passage-en-00583

Thus every quality of the barzakhs—every aspect and form appearing in bodies—is an effect of Light. The source that gives Light (Dator Luminum, the Giver of Lights) cannot itself be a barzakh. It must be something outside all dark substances and qualities.
III. The Zoroastrian Light of Glory (Xvarnah) and Angelology
passage-en-00584

A difficulty would remain here if Suhrawardi had not taken care to distance himself from the “dualist Magi,” and if the ancient Persian sages whose theosophy he sought to revive had not been so close to the “Chaldean” sages of sacred rites whom the Neoplatonists had adopted (see above, Chapter I, 2 and Chapter II, 1–2). For the barzakh, being essentially Darkness, continues to exist as such after the Light that is foreign to it has withdrawn. This dark substance, then, is neither sheer non-being nor merely a lack of being.
III. The Zoroastrian Light of Glory (Xvarnah) and Angelology
passage-en-00585

What is it? Where does it come from? Suhrawardi cannot answer as one of the “dualists” would, since he has explicitly rejected radical dualism as impious. He writes: “It belongs to perfect Light to be the cause of an imperfect Light.”
III. The Zoroastrian Light of Glory (Xvarnah) and Angelology
passage-en-00586

We can now see what this implies. As Light spreads and pours itself forth, it declines by stages until it reaches the West of its total extinction. The material body, the barzakh, is extinguished, dead Light, which another Light, exiling itself there, will temporarily bring to life. In governing that body, the exiled Light finds the means of its own redemption, the point from which it can rise in its “sacred ascent” and attain its transformations into glory.
III. The Zoroastrian Light of Glory (Xvarnah) and Angelology
passage-en-00587

What is now Darkness was therefore once itself a light, but a light that, in clinging to the furthest point of its own decline and fall, seems to have denied itself. This implies that if some Souls of Light tear themselves free from exile, there must have been a more profound and radical catastrophe, the one that degraded Light into its own pure negation. The Ismaili sacred drama presented this admirably as a catastrophe occurring at the level of the fullness of Light (see above, Chapter II, § 2). Its resolution was already assured when the “spiritual Adam” cast out his own Iblis-Ahriman. Here everything unfolds as a metaphysical process.
III. The Zoroastrian Light of Glory (Xvarnah) and Angelology
passage-en-00588
Suhrawardi will allude to the implicit drama that occurred in the soul’s pre-existence in some of his Mystical Narratives (see below, Chapters IV and V).
III. The Zoroastrian Light of Glory (Xvarnah) and Angelology
passage-en-00589
Yet no causal explanation of what appears through dark, inert, lifeless substance—whether the appearance lasts or is fleeting—can be based on that substance itself.
III. The Zoroastrian Light of Glory (Xvarnah) and Angelology
passage-en-00590

Consider two examples. If the oil in a lamp rises towards the flame, nothing has been explained, in Suhrawardi’s view, merely by invoking a physical law, whether the horror vacui, nature’s supposed abhorrence of a vacuum, or some active property of fire. Likewise, declares the shaykh al-Ishrâq, the sages of ancient Persia found it strange that anyone should suppose the marvellous colours of a peacock’s plumage to result simply from the bird’s bodily constitution, from some mixture or combination within its feathers, without any definite purpose or personally acting intelligence at work.
III. The Zoroastrian Light of Glory (Xvarnah) and Angelology
passage-en-00591

No: in both cases what is revealed is an intelligent ordering, the work of the Angel who is the “lord of the Species.” In the first case this is the guardian Angel of the cone of flame, the very Angel the Persians called Ordibehesht (Avestan Arta Vahishta). For the bodily species is like a shadow, a projection, an icon (sanam) of its Angel, a theurgy (tilism, Greek telesma) that the Angel works in the barzakh, which of itself is dead, absolute night. “The ancient Persians,” Suhrawardi reminds us, “were supremely expert and diligent in matters of angelology (fî arbâb al-anwâ’).
III. The Zoroastrian Light of Glory (Xvarnah) and Angelology
passage-en-00592
“Thus they gave special worship to the Angel they called Hômâ Izad, the Angel of haoma, the plant that played such a major role in their religious rites.”
III. The Zoroastrian Light of Glory (Xvarnah) and Angelology
passage-en-00593

So, too, throughout Suhrawardi’s writings we encounter, one after another, the names of the six Zoroastrian archangels—the Amâhraspands, the “Holy Immortals.” With Ohrmazd, their prince and source, they form the divine Heptad of Light and Wisdom. The commentators Qotboddin Shirazi and Shahrazuri draw attention to each of these names and add their own explanations. They carefully describe the relations between the group of three “masculine” archangels and that of three “feminine” archangels, and the particular theurgies through which each acts.
III. The Zoroastrian Light of Glory (Xvarnah) and Angelology
passage-en-00594

We are told again that the sage Zoroaster was admitted to contemplate them, to enter into union with the divine Heptad, and to receive initiation into higher knowledge from each of the Seven. All proceeded one from another “as one lamp is kindled from another without the light of the first being diminished in any way.”
III. The Zoroastrian Light of Glory (Xvarnah) and Angelology
passage-en-00595

We have already learned that the first Light to proceed from the Light of Lights is the sublime Light the ancient Persians called Bahman, identified with the First Intelligence in both the Avicennian and the Ismaili worlds of divine Intelligences. From this sublime Light proceeded Ordibehesht, the Angel of Fire. Next came Shahrîvar (Avestan Xshathra Vairya, “Desirable Dominion”), the Angel of the sun and the metals (see also § 5 below, on the sun as the theurgy of the Angel).
III. The Zoroastrian Light of Glory (Xvarnah) and Angelology
passage-en-00596

Then came Esfandarmoz (Avestan Spenta-Armaiti), the archangelic Light (Nûr qâhir) whose theurgy is the Earth, and whom the Mazdean texts hail as the “daughter of Ohrmazd.” The role of “mistress of the household” (kadbâ-nû’ya) that Suhrawardi recognises in her preserves a precise memory of this tradition. Elsewhere we have tried to show the importance of this figure in the spiritual life of ancient Iran and of Islamic Persia, even where she bears another name. In her person the Earth is transfigured.
III. The Zoroastrian Light of Glory (Xvarnah) and Angelology
passage-en-00597
Finally come the two archangels already named: Khordâd (Avestan Haurvatât), the Angel of Water, and Mordâd (Avestan Amertât, “Immortality”), the Angel of plants.
III. The Zoroastrian Light of Glory (Xvarnah) and Angelology
passage-en-00598

Our shaykh al-Ishrâq knows that these beings of light are also those whom Hermes, Agathodaimon, and Plato spoke of or were themselves allowed to contemplate. This, he says, is why they did not support their claims with rational proofs. Instead they laid claim to direct personal vision and offered their testimony. If they did so, our shaykh believes, it is not for us to dispute with them. His position, which we already know, remains consistent. In astronomy, the Peripatetic philosophers trust the observations of Ptolemy and those of the Chaldean astronomers.
III. The Zoroastrian Light of Glory (Xvarnah) and Angelology
passage-en-00599

Yet those very same Chaldean sages, like the sages of ancient Greece, claimed to have seen the realities of the spiritual world for themselves. Why trust their experience when it concerns observations of the physical world, but reject their experience when it concerns the spiritual world? What counts in one case must count in the other.
III. The Zoroastrian Light of Glory (Xvarnah) and Angelology
passage-en-00600

Here we truly have a vision of the world embracing the entire heavenly universe known to the sages of ancient Iran; it is also the meeting place of all the mystical theosophers invoked by Suhrawardi. We should not speak of “syncretism.” It is too easy a word, too often used either to discredit a teaching or to avoid examining it further. Anyone who considers only opinions combining or merging with other opinions will find it easy to speak of syncretism. Anyone who considers instead what those opinions are about, as it appears to the people who hold them, will be much more cautious.
III. The Zoroastrian Light of Glory (Xvarnah) and Angelology
passage-en-00601

Suhrawardi is not attempting a harmonious synthesis of philosophical opinions that happen to resemble one another. He starts from what he regards as an objective finding: the agreement of testimonies concerning the same reality. The spiritual world witnessed directly by the theosophers of different traditions is, for him, indeed the same world. That is what matters to him, and it is what matters to us here.
III. The Zoroastrian Light of Glory (Xvarnah) and Angelology
passage-en-00602

Bringing together a body of testimony is not “syncretism.” It does, however, presuppose that one “believes” in this spiritual world. Once that condition is recognised, we can see the meeting that takes place here between Zoroastrian angelology and the “Magian” wisdom of the Chaldean sages, those of the Oracles interpreted by the Neoplatonists. This is the meaning we sought earlier to bring out in Suhrawardi’s undertaking. Research should therefore examine the transformations Plato’s Ideas had already undergone in Chaldean-Neoplatonic theosophy, a considerable undertaking in itself.
III. The Zoroastrian Light of Glory (Xvarnah) and Angelology
passage-en-00603

The encounter between Chaldean practitioners of sacred rites and the metaphysics of Middle Platonism and Neoplatonism had already begun to work out the great solution Suhrawardi develops in full, adding the testimony of his own experience. That solution identifies the Platonic Ideas, the archetypes of Light (mothol aflatûniya nûriya), with the archangels and archangelic beings of Zoroastrianism. This identification is the major spiritual fact of his Eastern Theosophy.
III. The Zoroastrian Light of Glory (Xvarnah) and Angelology
passage-en-00604

A phenomenologist can only begin from that fact, seek to understand it, and uncover the intentions at work in it and the reality towards which they are directed. If one proceeds instead by arguing from abstract concepts, the difficulties become insoluble. Already in the eighth Islamic century (the fourteenth century CE), an unfortunately anonymous thinker had explained, in a learned dissertation, that Suhrawardi’s position no longer corresponded at all to the problem Plato had originally posed.
III. The Zoroastrian Light of Glory (Xvarnah) and Angelology
passage-en-00605

Suhrawardi’s angelology reflects the same vision as that of the Neoplatonists who interpreted the Chaldean sages. In this respect, the Khosrawânîyûn sages whose testimony he invokes are indeed the “Neoplatonists of Persia.”
III. The Zoroastrian Light of Glory (Xvarnah) and Angelology
passage-en-00606

We can already see this in the names given to the archetypal Angels. Each is the Angel or lord of a Species (rabb al-nû’), of its image or icon (sanam), of its theurgy (tilism). The bodily species itself is that theurgy, since it is the Angel’s own action. The concept of the archetype is no longer quite the one that posed a problem for us in classical Plato.
III. The Zoroastrian Light of Glory (Xvarnah) and Angelology
passage-en-00607

Instead, it shapes the whole religious devotion and spiritual life of the Ishrâqîyûn. This angelic interpretation of the Platonic Ideas—the ta’wîl, or spiritual interpretation, of the theory of Ideas—is, in effect, what Suhrawardi regards as the most precious inheritance from the theosophy of the ancient Persians. Every decision he makes in physics, psychology, cosmology, and metaphysics is directed towards preserving it.
III. The Zoroastrian Light of Glory (Xvarnah) and Angelology
passage-en-00608

But a difficulty remains: what kind of participation in being (methexis) connects the heavenly reality that is the Angel of a Species with the individuals that make up the material or earthly existence of that Species? In short, what foundation in being allows both Angel and species to share the same name?
III. The Zoroastrian Light of Glory (Xvarnah) and Angelology
passage-en-00609
Suhrawardi himself sums up his position in three propositions:
III. The Zoroastrian Light of Glory (Xvarnah) and Angelology
passage-en-00610
The Angel of each Species is a reality existing in its own right: a distinct spiritual individual, existing in and for itself.
III. The Zoroastrian Light of Glory (Xvarnah) and Angelology
passage-en-00611

There can be no question of an indwelling presence that would merge the Angel and its species into a single collective whole. Since the Angel of the Species is an Intelligence belonging to the world of Light, how could that Intelligence both exist as an individual in its own right and be present within the species and its many individual members?
III. The Zoroastrian Light of Glory (Xvarnah) and Angelology
passage-en-00612

Nor can we accept that the Angel of the human Species, for instance, exists because of and for the sake of what is beneath it. (The same applies to the “Pole,” the Imam as conceived in Shiism. As we know, his being the Imam depends in no way on whether human beings recognise him. The parallel is all the more compelling because a Shiite thinker such as Qazi Sa'id Qommi, who understood the Imam through the angelology of the Ishrâq, would describe him as the “lord of the Species” in relation to his faithful.) If an archetype meant no more than a model whose only purpose was to serve what exists below it, the archetypal Angel could no longer be called the “lord of the Species.” But Suhrawardi knows that the ancient sages never made that mistake.
III. The Zoroastrian Light of Glory (Xvarnah) and Angelology
passage-en-00613

For every species of plant, for example, there must be a spiritual being, separate from Matter and therefore endowed with knowledge and consciousness, which protects that species and cares for it as its guardian Angel. According to Suhrawardi, this is the being whom the ancient sages of Persia called the Angel or lord of that species (rabb al-nû’). The claim, of course, concerns every species that has a substantial existence of its own, not accidental or partial things.
III. The Zoroastrian Light of Glory (Xvarnah) and Angelology
passage-en-00614

All events in the life of plants, and likewise everything that occurs within a human being without the knowledge of the thinking soul, are governed by the Angel of the respective Species. This Angel must not be confused with the soul: a soul and its body together form a single individual. The higher a species stands in the hierarchy of being, the more intermediaries there are between it and its Angel.
III. The Zoroastrian Light of Glory (Xvarnah) and Angelology
passage-en-00615

In the human case, for example, there is the thinking soul and the subtle organs constituted by the three kinds of pneuma, or vital spirit. Suffering and injury to the body affect the soul that animates it, but they cannot affect the Angel. Neither the Angel of plants nor the Angel of fire, nor any of the other angelic lords, is injured by the violence inflicted on the species it governs. Their compassion for their respective species is not a matter of suffering but, essentially, of acting, as befits an Intelligence that is by nature fully actual and active.
III. The Zoroastrian Light of Glory (Xvarnah) and Angelology
passage-en-00616

Everything within a species that contributes to its coming into being and its continuing to exist proceeds from the activity of that Intelligence—from its acts of understanding and contemplation through which the species emanates. It is because the species is thus the contemplative activity of this Intelligence, its Angel, that the species is called the Angel’s theurgy.
III. The Zoroastrian Light of Glory (Xvarnah) and Angelology
passage-en-00617

It follows that the Angel of a Species, as archetype, appears as an archetypal person. Yet if its activity of understanding and contemplation causes a bodily species to emanate, that is in no way because the Angel needs the species. Such a need exists only for souls that must pass through the education of sensory knowledge—that is, through earthly existence—in order to attain their perfection.
III. The Zoroastrian Light of Glory (Xvarnah) and Angelology
passage-en-00618

But the law governing the descending hierarchy of being is strict and unchanging. A higher level does not find its perfection in a lower one. On the contrary, every level finds its perfected state in the Principle from which it emanates and which is its first cause. The species governed by the Angel is not the Angel’s ultimate purpose; rather, the Angel is the ultimate purpose of the species it governs, because the Angel is, in person, that species in its perfected state. This is the sense in which the Angel is its archetype. Its luminous nature is not something added to its essence, to its very selfhood, something it could acquire from below.
III. The Zoroastrian Light of Glory (Xvarnah) and Angelology
passage-en-00619

Certainly other Lights are continually added to its Light through the eternal manifestation of what is above in what is below. Human souls, too, are in their essential nature separate Lights and receptacles of sacred Lights; sensory perception merely prepares them to receive those higher Lights. The sages of ancient Persia knew this, unlike the “exotericists”—those concerned only with outward teachings—who remain bound to their books and never rise to the point of direct personal vision.
III. The Zoroastrian Light of Glory (Xvarnah) and Angelology
passage-en-00620

What, then, do the “Eastern” theosophers, the Khosrawânîyûn, mean when they speak of the Angel of a Species as the universal of that Species? They certainly cannot mean the universal as logic understands it: the general concept of a species, a concept whose very generality allows a multitude of individual beings to share in what it expresses. Such a concept is defined precisely by being negatively conditioned (bi-sharti lâ): it excludes any particular determination that would prevent all individuals of the same kind from falling under it.
III. The Zoroastrian Light of Glory (Xvarnah) and Angelology
passage-en-00621
But Eastern Theosophy understands the Angels of the Species as independently existing realities of Light, each possessing its own distinct spiritual identity, in which no other being can participate.
III. The Zoroastrian Light of Glory (Xvarnah) and Angelology
passage-en-00622
Thus, when we grasp the concept of a Species, it does not follow that we have grasped the Angel of that Species. In what sense, then, can the species be said to participate in its Angel?
III. The Zoroastrian Light of Glory (Xvarnah) and Angelology
passage-en-00623

We can understand this participation only by recognizing that the Angel, as a distinct spiritual reality, brings forth the material species through its thought, through its contemplative activity, as an act of theurgy—a spiritual act of creation. All the natural relationships and proportions observable in the embodied species are the shadow, image, or icon (sanam) of the spiritual relationships and forms of light existing within the Angel's own being, its own “person,” and its activity of thought. The individual material being is short-lived; it is the species as a whole that preserves this Image continuously.
III. The Zoroastrian Light of Glory (Xvarnah) and Angelology
passage-en-00624

The Angel is therefore universal—a metaphysical universal—in the sense that it is the “Mother of the Species” (Omm al-nû’). As such, it stands in the same relationship to the species as a whole and to each of its members, because it is the “Lord of that Species” (rabb al-nû’): the being that bestows its perfections and guides the species by guiding its countless individuals.
III. The Zoroastrian Light of Glory (Xvarnah) and Angelology
passage-en-00625

The Angel is determined only by what it is in itself, by the being it receives from its Principle. It is determined neither by the generality of the concept of the species nor by one particular feature of fleeting material existence rather than another. That is why the Angel of humanity appears to each human being in a form individual to that person: as that person's own Perfect Nature, their own guardian Angel.
III. The Zoroastrian Light of Glory (Xvarnah) and Angelology
passage-en-00626

If, then, the Angel of a Species is called its universal, and if the same name is applied to both the Angel and the species, this is because their relationship resembles that between the image appearing in a mirror and the person standing before it. Here again we encounter concepts fundamental to all Islamic gnosis, as we have already seen in Shiite teachings concerning the Imam: mazhar and mazhariya, the form in which something manifests itself—as in a mirror—and that form's power to make a higher reality appear.
III. The Zoroastrian Light of Glory (Xvarnah) and Angelology
passage-en-00627
It follows that the Angel is the universal of the species over which it presides because its care extends equally to the whole species and to each of its members.
III. The Zoroastrian Light of Glory (Xvarnah) and Angelology
passage-en-00628

Moreover, as an absolute archetypal person—absolute in the sense that nothing determines its luminous spiritual identity except the Principle from which it derives—the Angel presents to the whole species, and to every one of its individuals, the goal toward which they tend: their complete and perfected state. The Angel of the Species is the being in whom everything required by its nature is already fully realized, the being whose ever-renewed desire is forever fulfilled by the presence of what it desires.
III. The Zoroastrian Light of Glory (Xvarnah) and Angelology
passage-en-00629

This explains the Hermetic designation “complete,” “fulfilled,” or “perfect” (tâmm), given to the “Perfect Nature” that appears to Hermes in a vision and to which Suhrawardi dedicates one of the psalms in his “Book of Hours.” Compare the designation “Perfect Man,” Insân kâmil, Greek anthrôpos teleios. It also explains why Suhrawardi so firmly rejects the idea that the primary purpose of the archetypal Lights is merely to serve as models for the creation of species and individuals. That would make these higher beings subordinate to the lower existences they govern—beings that are themselves the products of their theurgic activity and the images in which they appear.
III. The Zoroastrian Light of Glory (Xvarnah) and Angelology
passage-en-00630

The relationship is precisely the reverse. The lower beings owe their existence to the archetypal reality of the higher Light, and from that Light they receive both the dignity and the purpose of their own existence: to become the image and expression of their Angel, insofar as they strive to attain its “perfect state.”
III. The Zoroastrian Light of Glory (Xvarnah) and Angelology
passage-en-00631

In short, the relationship between a species and the Angel that is its Perfect Nature becomes clearest if we return to the words of the psalm Suhrawardi dedicates to that Angel, translated below in § 5, or if we recall the “prayer of the heliotrope,” so beautifully described by Proclus.
III. The Zoroastrian Light of Glory (Xvarnah) and Angelology
passage-en-00632

When these Lights are called “Platonic Ideas or archetypes of light” (mothol aflatûniya nûriya), Species existing in a state of light (Anwâ’ nûriya), each possessing the nature of an angelic spiritual reality, Suhrawardi may not be expressing precisely what Plato himself intended. His thought is, however, entirely in harmony with that of the Neoplatonists. At the same time, it brings us close to the Avestan and Zoroastrian concept of the ratu, a term designating the guardian Angels of beings in heaven and on earth. We have already noted that Suhrawardi gives Esfandarmoz, the Angel of the Earth, the specifically Avestan title kadbânû, “mistress of the house.”
III. The Zoroastrian Light of Glory (Xvarnah) and Angelology
passage-en-00633

But there is more. As we shall shortly recall, the Angel of humanity is none other than Gabriel, the Holy Spirit, the “Active Intellect” of the philosophers. When this Angel's relationship to a particular human being takes on an individual form, the Angel appears to that person as their “Perfect Nature.” Now, as we noted earlier, Qâzî Sa’îd Qommî, a great seventeenth-century Shiite theosopher, makes a striking comparison in his commentary on a famous sermon of the First Imam. He sees the relationship between the Imam and each faithful believer as corresponding to the relationship between the Holy Spirit, Lord of the human Species, and the soul of each initiate, for whom the Spirit is the “Perfect Nature.”
III. The Zoroastrian Light of Glory (Xvarnah) and Angelology
passage-en-00634

The philosophical devotion of the Ishrâqî tradition and Shiite devotion to the Imam thus share a fundamental feature of Iranian Islamic spirituality, whose roots we can also discover in certain forms of ancient Gnosis. The multiplication of theophanic relationships—relationships through which the divine becomes manifest—expresses a mystical devotion that seeks neither emptiness nor formlessness, but a unifying relationship between persons. In doing so, it is equally concerned to preserve tawhîd, the oneness of God and the absolute transcendence of the One beyond all others.
III. The Zoroastrian Light of Glory (Xvarnah) and Angelology
en-book-2-ch-3-s4
4. The Hierarchies of the Archangelic Lights
III. The Zoroastrian Light of Glory (Xvarnah) and Angelology
passage-en-00635

This broad picture, briefly sketched, allows us to understand the structure of Suhrawardi's angelology and to see exactly where it breaks with the Peripatetic or Avicennian system. Suhrawardi himself revealed the decisive moment of that break in his account of the vision of the Light of Glory (above, p. 99).
III. The Zoroastrian Light of Glory (Xvarnah) and Angelology
passage-en-00636

In Avicenna's system, the emergence of multiplicity begins with the first of the Cherubic Intellects (Karûbîyûn) and with the three acts of understanding that constitute its being. It understands its Principle; it understands its own existence as made necessary by that Principle; and it understands that, considered apart from its Principle, its own existence is merely possible and could just as well not be. These three acts of contemplation take on distinct realities respectively as a second Intellect, a first Angel-Soul that moves the outermost celestial sphere, and that first Heaven itself.
III. The Zoroastrian Light of Glory (Xvarnah) and Angelology
passage-en-00637

In fact, Avicenna seems to have hesitated for a long time over the structure of the angelic world that ought to be inferred, after the fact, from astronomical observations. Whether one accepted Aristotle's celestial physics or Ptolemy's theory, should one posit no more than ten Intellects? Or, following Aristotle, should there be somewhat more than fifty, corresponding to the additional celestial spheres needed to explain the irregularities in planetary motion?
III. The Zoroastrian Light of Glory (Xvarnah) and Angelology
passage-en-00638

It was the inadequacy of this scheme that Suhrawardi's vision of the “Sources of the Light of Glory” revealed to him. From then on, rather than confining himself to our solar system and deriving from it a set of nested celestial spheres—whether Aristotle's concentric spheres or Ptolemy's epicycles and eccentric circles—he directed his contemplation above all toward the “Heaven of the Fixed Stars,” whose explanation had already created more than one difficulty for celestial physics. He reflected on the almost infinite multitude of individual stars suggested by this eighth Heaven—that is, all the worlds beyond our solar system—and came to see that the mystery of how being becomes multiple must be sought among these wonders.
III. The Zoroastrian Light of Glory (Xvarnah) and Angelology
passage-en-00639

Earlier philosophers had failed to make sufficient use of the contemplative and loving activity of the Intellects to explain the emergence of these innumerable beings. Even the two intellectual “dimensions” recognized by the Peripatetics in each Intellect, necessity and possibility, were inadequate when considered in terms of desire. Suhrawardi even sensed that beyond the “Heaven of the Fixed Stars” there must be other universes, more marvelous still. The angelology whose necessity he grasped by intuition, a priori, could have matched the staggering dimensions calculated by modern astronomy. This stands in contrast to what happened during the astronomical revolution in the West, which did away with angelology.
III. The Zoroastrian Light of Glory (Xvarnah) and Angelology
passage-en-00640
Suhrawardi's angelology takes shape in three stages:
III. The Zoroastrian Light of Glory (Xvarnah) and Angelology
passage-en-00641

1) From the eternal coming-into-being of the Firstborn Light, proceeding from the Light of Lights—a Light he identifies with Bahman, the first of the Zoroastrian archangels proceeding from Ohrmazd—Suhrawardi abandons the two or three intellectual “dimensions” available to Peripatetic angelology. In that earlier system, three acts of contemplation repeat themselves from one Intellect to the next as each proceeds from its predecessor.
III. The Zoroastrian Light of Glory (Xvarnah) and Angelology
passage-en-00642

In their place, Suhrawardi introduces a plurality of “dimensions” that inform his entire “Eastern Theosophy.” There are the dimensions called qahr and mahabbat, dominion and love, arising from his very conception of the Light of Glory. There are independence and dependence; there are the specifically “Eastern” dimensions of contemplation and illumination—contemplation that “rises toward” a higher Light and illumination that “rises upon” a lower one. There are also irradiation and reflection, and so on. Through these many-sided relationships, the multiplication of distinct beings of Light rapidly becomes innumerable.
III. The Zoroastrian Light of Glory (Xvarnah) and Angelology
passage-en-00643

At the highest, invisible level, these dimensions seem to enact the laws of optics: they combine with one another, and the ways in which they participate in one another, together with the proportions of that participation, produce a complexity without limit. Each individual Light, arising from these multiple irradiations and reflections, receives them from every Light that precedes it and communicates them to every Light that follows it, both directly and through the mediation of all the others.
III. The Zoroastrian Light of Glory (Xvarnah) and Angelology
passage-en-00644

The increasing complexity and accelerating rhythm defy the imagination's efforts to follow or measure them. In this way the universe of “Primordial Archangelic Lights” proceeds eternally. Because these Lights give rise to one another in a hierarchy of causes, they form a descending order, which Suhrawardi calls the Longitudinal Order (tabaqat al-Tûl). This is the universe of archangels he calls the Sovereign Lights, the Supreme Sources (al-Osûl al-A’âlîn), or the “World of the Mothers” (al-Ommahât).
III. The Zoroastrian Light of Glory (Xvarnah) and Angelology
passage-en-00645

2) The hierarchy of the archangelic “World of the Mothers” gives rise to two distinct orders within the fullness of the world of Light. This results from the two categories of “dimensions” that constitute the archangels' being. One category may be called positive. The other expresses a lack: the dependence inherent in every Light whose being does not belong to it by its own right but comes from its Principle.
III. The Zoroastrian Light of Glory (Xvarnah) and Angelology
passage-en-00646

From the first category—dominion, independence, active illumination, and contemplation—proceeds a second order of archangels, or “Victorious Lights.” These no longer cause one another's existence or stand in a relationship of subordination. Instead, they correspond to one another and stand on equal terms. They form the Latitudinal Order (tabaqat al-’Ard). These are the archetypal archangels, the “Lords of the Species”—either masculine, arbâb al-anwâ’, or feminine, rabbât al-anwâ’—the Angels whose spiritual activity brings forth all the Species of the sensible and imaginal worlds.
III. The Zoroastrian Light of Glory (Xvarnah) and Angelology
passage-en-00647

We have already examined their manner of existence. They are in no sense abstract concepts treated as though they were independently existing things. They are genuinely independent angelic realities, existing in and for themselves. Their universality consists in the outpouring of their light upon all the beings that make up the Species born of their contemplation, and in the care they extend to every one of those beings.
III. The Zoroastrian Light of Glory (Xvarnah) and Angelology
passage-en-00648

From the second category of intelligible dimensions within the primordial archangels of the “World of the Mothers”—those expressing dependence, such as love and longing for the higher Light, reliance upon it, and the illumination received from it—proceeds the “Heaven of the Fixed Stars,” which serves as their common form of manifestation. The countless individual stars and constellations are emanations that give material form, in celestial matter—a still-subtle materia prima, or primary matter—to the element of non-being contained in those archangels' existence, if we imagine that existence separated from the Light of Lights, which eternally establishes its necessity to be.
III. The Zoroastrian Light of Glory (Xvarnah) and Angelology
passage-en-00649

For Avicenna's followers, the motion of the Heaven of the Fixed Stars arises from the longing of the single Soul that moves this Heaven for the single Intellect from which that Soul proceeds. The subtle matter of this Heaven marks the distance between the Soul's longing and the object of its longing. For Suhrawardi, the innumerable wonders of the Heaven of the Fixed Stars already demand a corresponding multiplication of Intellects and Souls.
III. The Zoroastrian Light of Glory (Xvarnah) and Angelology
passage-en-00650

3) From the second order of archangels, the Latitudinal Order—the Lords of the celestial Species in the starry universe and of the elemental Species in our sublunary world—proceeds a further Order of Lights. Through these Lights the archetypal Archangels govern the Species. Whereas the Lights of the first two categories are called “Victorious” (Anwâr qâhira), those of the third are called “Governing Lights” (Anwâr modabbira). They are the Angel-Souls.
III. The Zoroastrian Light of Glory (Xvarnah) and Angelology
passage-en-00651

More significantly still, as we have already noted, the shaykh al-Ishrâq gives the Lights of this hierarchy an ancient Iranian title of command and knighthood: the Espahbad Lights. The name calls to mind the Stoic hêgemon or hegemonikon, the ruling principle, but the setting in which Suhrawardi places it is still more revealing. It evokes the heroic epic of Iranian chivalry and also the battle that has raged since the beginning of the world, described in the first chapter of the Bundahishn, the Mazdean book of Genesis.
III. The Zoroastrian Light of Glory (Xvarnah) and Angelology
passage-en-00652

The Espahbad Lights are thinking, governing souls; they are guides and interpreters—compare the Greek exègètès, meaning both a guide and an interpreter, a hermeneut. Each human soul is such a Light. So too are the Lights that move the celestial spheres and govern the Species present within those spheres, serving as intermediaries of the archetypal Archangel of which each Species is the icon or theurgic manifestation.
III. The Zoroastrian Light of Glory (Xvarnah) and Angelology
passage-en-00653

Each Species is at once the instrument and the setting of the “battle” undertaken by its Espahbad Light so that the power of the Light from which it proceeds may triumph. In Suhrawardi's system, the Espahbad Light thus assumes the role of the Zoroastrian Fravartis (forûhar), who “choose” to descend into the material world to fight against Darkness. When the outcome of this struggle—fought “for the Angel”—takes the form of the “rising” of the Espahbad Light, triumphantly emerging from its “West” and returning upright to its “East,” the heroic epic becomes a mystical epic.
III. The Zoroastrian Light of Glory (Xvarnah) and Angelology
passage-en-00654

We shall see later (Chapter IV, § 3 onward, and Chapter V) that this transformation may be the deepest meaning of ta’wîl, spiritual interpretation: the act that restores the world of ancient Persia's Light to Islamic gnosis. It may be the very meaning of Suhrawardi's work.
III. The Zoroastrian Light of Glory (Xvarnah) and Angelology
passage-en-00655

Such, in broad outline, is Suhrawardi's angelology. There are, in summary, three great orders of Lights, the “Victorious” or Dominating Lights (Anwâr qâhira, al-Qawâhir) being divided into two orders.
